opus-5.5.text:
Thanks for having me. It's a question I've thought about quite a bit, because from the outside it can look like a sharp turn: someone who spent years thinking about very fundamental questions suddenly cares about products, teams, funding, and timelines.

From where I sit, it's less a change of identity than a change of leverage. A good scientist is always asking, "What is the most important problem I can make progress on, and what's the best tool for making that progress?" For a long time the answer was a paper, a theory, a group of students. In AI right now, many of the most important questions can't be answered with a whiteboard and a few GPUs. You need large-scale experiments, engineering infrastructure, and people working full-time on one direction for years. Sometimes the only practical way to assemble that is to build an organization, and in many cases that means a company.

There's also a sense of urgency. In physics, if you're right about something, it will still be right in fifty years, so there's no rush. With AI, the technology is moving fast and shaping society now. If you believe a certain approach is important, whether for capability, interpretability, or safety, you can't wait for the field to slowly come around. You have to show it working, and showing it working often looks like entrepreneurship.

That said, I don't think the scientific mindset goes away. The best scientist-founders treat the company as a big experiment: there's a hypothesis about how things should be built, and the company is how you test it against reality. Reality is a much harsher reviewer than any referee, and I think that's part of the appeal.

For me as a student, it's been instructive. It made me realize that the boundary between "doing science" and "building things" is much blurrier than I thought. The question isn't scientist or entrepreneur. The question is: what problem do you care about, and what form does your work need to take to actually move it forward?

fable-5.1.text:
Honestly, I wasn't that surprised. If you've worked with Max for a few years, you know he doesn't really draw a hard line between "doing science" and "doing something about it." He's always been someone who starts from a very big question — what is intelligence, how do we make it understandable, how do we make sure it goes well for humanity — and then asks what the most effective lever is right now. For a long time the answer was writing papers and running a lab. I think at some point he looked at how fast things were moving in AI and concluded that academic papers alone weren't going to shift the trajectory much. If the thing you care about is the outcome in the world rather than the paper count, going out and building something is a pretty natural step.

The way I'd put it is that he's not changing what he cares about, he's changing the instrument. In the lab we spent a lot of time on interpretability, on trying to make models that are transparent, that you can actually read like you read a physics equation. That work is genuinely exciting intellectually, but it has a weakness: a result that lives in an arXiv paper only matters if someone with real systems picks it up. When you build a company, you get to put those ideas into something people actually use, and you get feedback that you'd never get from a reviewer. I think he found that appealing — and maybe also found that he had a kind of impatience that academia doesn't reward.

For me personally, it's also a bit of a mirror. As a student you often have this binary in your head: either you're a "real" scientist and you stay pure, or you "sell out" and go to industry. Watching him made me realize that's a false dichotomy. The best scientists I know are driven by curiosity and by wanting their understanding to touch reality. Those two things don't have to live in different buildings. I still consider myself a scientist first — I like the slow, careful work of understanding why something works, not just that it works. But I don't see entrepreneurship as a betrayal of that. If anything, I think the AI field needs more people who carry a scientist's standards of honesty and rigor into building things, rather than fewer.

And of course there's a practical side: the gap between research and product in AI has gotten so small now that the roles are blurring anyway. A lot of frontier research happens inside companies because that's where the compute and the data are. So someone like him moving in that direction is also just a reflection of where the field's center of gravity has gone. I'd rather have people who've spent decades thinking seriously about risk and interpretability inside that center than standing outside commenting on it.

astra-6.text:
I see it as a change in how you pursue an idea. As a scientist, you’re mostly asking, “Is this true? Can we understand why it works?” As an entrepreneur, you also have to ask, “Can we turn this into something people actually use?” Those questions are connected, but they require different kinds of work.

I can’t speak for all of my advisor’s motivations, but I can understand the appeal of taking that next step. Once you see a promising direction, you may want to build the team and the organization that can make it real. To me, that doesn’t necessarily mean leaving the scientific mindset behind. It means bringing it into a setting where you also have to deal with customers, resources, and execution.

As an entrepreneur, you try to turn those possibilities into something people can actually use. That brings a different set of challenges: building a team, understanding what people need, and making decisions under uncertainty. So I don’t necessarily see it as leaving science behind. It can also be a way of taking the work further.
